content:
At our family farm, Serra Branca, a useful AI conversation starts with ordinary questions: how much milk was recorded today, which cows are lactating in a particular location, or how one animal’s production changed over a period. The answers already belong to our operational systems. The challenge is making them accessible in a conversation while preserving their meaning and access rules.
That is the starting point of Anmar’s agent platform. As of late October, a private Telegram assistant can consult milk production, herd summaries and production by animal, as well as historical statistics and comparisons. The broader plan includes specialists for milking, herd management, dairy production and sales. Today, the deployed pilot is one assistant, in one private conversation, with milk and herd tools connected.
The applications come before the agent Anmar has separate applications for farm operations, including milk, herd, cheese production and sales. They remain responsible for operational records and business rules. The assistant reads the relevant APIs through tools with deliberately limited interfaces.
This distinction becomes concrete in a question like “how many cows produced milk today?” Milk records can answer how many distinct animals have recorded production for that date. The herd application answers which animals are currently classified as lactating. Those are different populations. Adding the morning and afternoon animal counts would also count some cows twice.
Offline operation adds another boundary: a shift marked closed on the server does not prove that every device has synchronized. Missing records do not automatically mean zero production. The tool returns coverage and state alongside the values so the conversation can preserve those distinctions.
Architecture: one worker, several controlled boundaries The deployed Telegram worker calls Agno directly. AgentOS also provides an authenticated HTTP interface for local execution and tests; it is not a public hop in the deployed chat path.
Component Role in this implementation Python 3.12 and Agno 3.1.10 Compose the assistant, tools, instructions and personal memory. Telegram worker Accept the linked private chat, persist incoming work and deliver responses. LiteLLM Route OpenAI-compatible requests through configured model aliases and a scoped key with budget and rate controls. DeepSeek pilot Generate responses and tool calls; configured free fallbacks remain separate choices. Anmar Apps and anmar-auth Issue short-lived integration tokens and validate access at each operational app. Milk and herd APIs Supply current records, domain calculations, identities and historical analysis. SQLite Persist agent sessions/preferences and the channel’s inbox/delivery state in separate databases. Docker and Coolify on Oracle infrastructure Run the ARM64 worker with persistent storage and supervised restart. The model connection follows LiteLLM’s OpenAI-compatible client interface. Provider selection belongs to gateway configuration; farm authorization remains in application code.
From a question to an answer The worker receives a message from the linked Telegram user and chat, and records it before processing. Agno receives the question, a bounded conversation history, the current capabilities and the required domain instructions. The model requests a tool. The tool supplies the configured identity and farm scope, obtains an integration token and calls the relevant API. Credentials and farm authorization are not arguments chosen by the model. The tool returns structured values with the relevant period, animal identity and coverage. Domain code performs calculations and validates consistency. The model writes a response, and the worker persists the response and delivery outcome. For an individual cow, the tool resolves the name or ear tag through Rebanho, then queries Leite. Repeated names require clarification. Historical analysis keeps the period and metric explicit; an average over days with records is not silently presented as an average over every calendar day.
A running process still needs a valid identity The first deployment exposed a simple operational failure: the bot remained running, but the human session it used to consult milk expired. Restarting the container could not repair that authentication boundary.
We replaced the human session with integration credentials. Anmar Apps issues five-minute tokens through Client Credentials; the client caches the bearer in memory and renews it before expiry. Each connected module has its own credential and audience, and the receiving app allows specific routes, methods and farm scope.
The Telegram identity and the API identity now have separate jobs. The first determines who may talk to this private pilot. The second determines what the software may read. Adding a new skill does not grant access to another farm or application.
Memory is for preferences; tools are for facts The assistant can save an explicitly requested presentation preference and recover it in a later session. This is persistent user memory, not model training. Agno’s agentic memory mechanism supplies a tool for memory updates; our instructions restrict its purpose to durable preferences.
Milk totals, herd counts, permissions and business rules must come from the systems. A previous answer is not a fresh reading. We found a practical example after repairing authentication: an existing conversation still contained the old access error, and the model repeated that the integration was unavailable without calling the tool.
The fix supplies the backend’s current capabilities alongside each new question. Replaying the old conversation then produced a fresh API call. It also showed why a successful test in a new session does not cover the experience of someone returning to a long-running conversation.
Domain procedures live in versioned SKILL.md files. An early test with optional loading called the milk tool but skipped its procedure and misdescribed a shift. Loading the relevant instructions into the initial context improved that case. Authorization, arithmetic and state validation still belong to deterministic code.
Limits and delivery are part of the product Short conversations worked with the initial free provider, but consecutive questions hit its token limit. The current DeepSeek pilot followed a small comparison of response behavior and availability, not a broad benchmark. Changing providers also changes data-retention assumptions; zero data retention has not been established for this pilot.
The worker now queues eligible transient model rate-limit failures, with up to four total attempts, preserving order and state across restarts. Credential and budget errors do not enter that retry loop. Runs involving memory tools are protected from automatic repetition. Context is limited to three completed rounds, with older tool results summarized while keeping useful parameters.
Telegram delivery has a different failure policy. A confirmed rate limit can retry the saved response. A connection failure with an unknown delivery outcome is recorded as uncertain rather than blindly sending the message again.
What is working, and what is still ahead The October 28 delivery records a complete run of 236 automated tests, followed by focused checks after review. The tests exercise real runtime and storage boundaries with controlled external responses. Separate acceptance checks used real APIs and models; those answer different questions from deterministic tests and do not establish unrestricted answer accuracy.
The private bot, milk/herd queries, historical analysis, integration-token renewal and bounded retry handling are deployed. The five named specialist bots and directors’ group access remain planned. Proactive milk alerts have a deterministic monitoring foundation, but delivery is not activated. The virtual-farm interface and knowledge-base integration are also future work; the current assistant is not backed by a deployed document-retrieval service.
The most useful progress has been making an ordinary farm question travel through clear boundaries: a known person, an authorized tool, a current record and an answer whose limitations can be explained.
summary:
At our family farm, Serra Branca, a useful AI conversation starts with ordinary questions: how much milk was recorded today, which cows are lactating in a particular location, or how one animal’s production changed over a period. The answers already belong to our operational systems. The challenge is making them accessible in a conversation while preserving their meaning and access rules.

That is the starting point of Anmar’s agent platform. As of late October, a private Telegram assistant can consult milk production, herd summaries and production by animal, as well as historical statistics and comparisons. The broader plan includes specialists for milking, herd management, dairy production and sales. Today, the deployed pilot is one assistant, in one private conversation, with milk and herd tools connected.
title: AI on the Farm: Connecting Conversation to Real Operations

content:
A sale of cheese at Anmar already has useful structure: a customer, individually identified pieces, weights, prices and payment records. Preparing the fiscal document introduces another set of responsibilities: issuer identity, tax configuration, numbering, certificates and the result returned by the authorization service.
We decided to build that boundary as a separate TribeSolutions product, with Anmar as its first customer. The intended entry points are a standalone operator portal and an integration API. Inventory, production and payments remain in the operational applications.
This is a development account, not a launch announcement. The local portal already supports registrations, draft preparation, PDF previews, offline XML signing and controlled recovery tests. No invoice has been transmitted to or authorized by Sefaz through this product. The integration API and the connection to Anmar Vendas are still planned.
A deliberately narrow first use case The agreed pilot concerns Anmar’s internal sales in Roraima, starting with its own queijo coalho production. The product’s initial target is goods invoices, NF-e model 55. Interstate sales, transfers, returns and other invoice models are outside this first slice.
A narrow scope lets us ask concrete questions about one workflow without pretending that a reference invoice defines every future transaction. Fiscal configuration is explicit, reviewed and versioned. The software does not infer a company’s full tax treatment from a PDF or fill unknown fields just to make a preview work.
Architecture: keep fiscal work behind one application boundary Solid boxes describe the local implementation. Dashed boxes are planned integrations. SOAP/HTTPS adapter code exists, but the application’s default transport is disabled.
Technology Why it is here PHP 8.5 and Laravel 13 Application services, authentication, forms, authorization and transactions. Blade and CSS A server-rendered portal for operators, without a separate frontend application. PostgreSQL 17 Organization data, draft versions, number allocations, attempts and audit records. NFePHP sped-nfe 5.2.8 XML construction and signing in the implemented offline flow. NFePHP sped-da DANFE preview generation from prepared XML. brick/math Exact decimal arithmetic for quantities, prices and rounding. OpenSSL and phpseclib Certificate inspection and certificate-chain work. Docker, PHPUnit and Laravel Pint Reproducible local services, behavior tests and formatting checks. NFePHP’s own guide describes XML creation, signing and communication facilities. Those capabilities are building blocks: adopting the library does not establish that our issuer, configuration or application is ready for authorization.
Isolation starts before a draft exists The portal has organization membership and roles for administration, operation and consultation. Platform administration does not automatically grant access to a customer’s invoices; support also needs explicit membership. Server-side services check that scope when loading and modifying records.
Authentication uses Argon2id passwords, encrypted database sessions, CSRF protection and login rate limits. Invitations are short-lived, single-use links whose tokens are stored as hashes. The current invitation flow copies links manually; it does not imply an email-delivery service.
Each issuer also has separate fiscal-environment configuration. Test preparation and production are distinct contexts throughout the model, not merely labels placed on the final page.
A draft is a versioned record of what the operator reviewed Drafts retain copies of the issuer, recipient, product and selected fiscal-profile data. Editing the catalog later does not silently rewrite what the operator reviewed. Refreshing those copies is an explicit action, and the typed price is preserved.
Updates carry a version. If another tab has changed the draft, the older form is rejected as a conflict while preserving the operator’s input. This prevents an apparently successful save from erasing a newer review.
Quantities and prices use decimal arithmetic. A commercial subtotal is kept distinct from a validated fiscal total; missing coverage or unconfirmed configuration remains visible as a pending condition.
That separation also changed the preview experience. Initially, the familiar DANFE preview belonged to a prepared, numbered test request. An operator trying fictitious registrations could not reach it without completing fiscal prerequisites. We added a simpler commercial draft PDF that requires neither an A1 certificate nor a reserved number. It is clearly identified as having no fiscal value. The DANFE preview remains a separate step derived from XML.
Protecting the A1 is a separate responsibility An A1 file and its password are encrypted together using AES-256-GCM, with a dedicated vault key supplied outside the database. Ordinary portal views do not need to expose that material. Offline inspection checks whether the key can be used, certificate dates and the issuer identity encoded in the certificate.
Certificate-chain and revocation checks are separate from opening the file or verifying a signature. The implementation includes offline checking and trust-material tooling, but an operational trust package and the real issuer’s readiness still need to be established before the first external test. A successful synthetic certificate test is evidence about the code path, not about a customer’s real certificate.
A timeout must not become another invoice The most consequential failure case is a request whose response is lost. The application cannot safely conclude that the remote service rejected it. Preparing a new request with a new number would obscure the original attempt and could create a second document.
The local implementation preserves request identity, version, numbering and attempts. Database transactions and locks protect allocations and concurrent operations. Controlled simulations exercise a lost response followed by consultation, repeated requests, competing processes and interruption during processing.
The response reader also checks correlation: environment, invoice key, signed XML digest and protocol context must agree before it classifies a response as authorization evidence. Ambiguous or unsupported returns remain candidates for reconciliation. That classification alone does not establish trusted delivery from a real authorization service.
SOAP and mutual-TLS HTTPS adapters exist behind a transport interface. The application currently binds that interface to a disabled transport. This lets us test the recovery logic and preserve original payloads without accidentally treating local preparation as a transmission.
Evidence so far, and the next boundary The latest recorded local suite passed 258 tests with 4,212 assertions. Browser checks covered synthetic organizations on desktop and mobile; PDF previews were inspected separately. These results come from the implementation checkpoints, and were not rerun merely to write this article.
The first external homologation test is still ahead. It requires the real issuer’s readiness, the appropriate certificate trust material, current official technical requirements and an explicitly enabled transmission/consultation flow. Production issuance, the public integration API, Anmar integration and operational deployment remain later milestones. Some of the current implementation is still local development work, beyond the last published branch commit.
Keeping the fiscal product separate makes its responsibility clear: prepare, submit and track a fiscal document with an auditable outcome. A future invoice cancellation must not silently reverse cheese inventory or payment records. Those operations belong to their own systems and require their own decisions.
summary:
A sale of cheese at Anmar already has useful structure: a customer, individually identified pieces, weights, prices and payment records. Preparing the fiscal document introduces another set of responsibilities: issuer identity, tax configuration, numbering, certificates and the result returned by the authorization service.

We decided to build that boundary as a separate TribeSolutions product, with Anmar as its first customer. The intended entry points are a standalone operator portal and an integration API. Inventory, production and payments remain in the operational applications.
title: Building an Invoice Platform: From a Sales Record to a Fiscal Document

content:
I had made games before, back when I was in college, but the idea for this one came during the pandemic. Dominoes are popular across Northern Brazil, including a point-scoring variant played in many homes. Galim is simply the name we gave this kind of game, not the name of the broader game category. Ralph and I play it with a set of regional rules, and turning those rules into software meant making each detail explicit: when a player may pass, how a hand ends, and how the score is credited.
The local table: one human player, three bots, and a score that can be traced back to each action.
The published game is available at galim.tribesolutions.com.br.
October update: a table that survives beyond one session Galim now has two ways to play. Single player keeps the local game against three bots, without requiring an account. Multiplayer lets one to four people sign in with Google and join the same room from their own phones or computers, filling the remaining seats with bots. The online version is deployed through Coolify. After testing it with our group, the next work focused on what happens around the moves: watching on a TV, reconnecting, leaving, finding a table and keeping results.
A room does not need to wait for another person. Its creator can fill the remaining seats with the existing characters — Tati, Bruno da ZL, or Rod do Alvorada — and change or remove those bots before starting. The table still has four seats and two partnerships. Players sitting opposite each other are partners. An online table with three bots still depends on the server and a connection.
The interface changes came from playing the game: controls are more compact, valid destinations are highlighted, and the rooster control for announcing a galo sits beside the player’s hand. After a confirmed galo, the three passes are presented together before the player continues. The announcement still has to happen before playing the tile; the presentation does not change the scoring rules.
Start with the rules The game uses the standard 28 dominoes, dealt into four hands of seven, with no draw pile. Partners sit opposite each other. Players score from the open ends of the board in multiples of five, and the starting double can open four paths through the board.
There are several details around that core. A hand can end with a player playing their last tile (batida) or when the game is blocked (fechamento). The galo and announcements of multiple doubles add further rules and scoring choices. The match checks its target score only after the hand has been fully scored.
Encoding these decisions in a TypeScript engine gave the rules a single place to live. The engine validates tile ownership, matching sides, orientation, legal destinations, passes, and end-of-hand behavior. Explicit rule options keep variants visible instead of hiding them in interface code.
Make the table playable The local React table lets one person play against three bots: a partner and two opponents. Each bot has a selectable difficulty. The easier bots choose among legal moves, while the more advanced profile considers immediate points and possible replies using only public information and its own hand.
The interface handles announcements, automatic turns, scoring, hand history, and mobile layouts. Only the human player’s hand is visible during play; the other hands are revealed when the hand ends so the result can be checked.
Single-player architecture: the game runs in the browser The playable local version is a React application built with Vite. Its TypeScript rules engine lives under server/src/game, but the web application imports that code directly into its browser bundle. The directory name does not mean that a move makes a network request: the local table executes the engine in the player’s browser.
The current local mode. Arrows inside the browser represent function calls and state updates, not HTTP requests.
The responsibilities are split across a few concrete components:
Component Responsibility React table Collect the selected tile and destination; display turns, feedback, board and score. Match Coordinate successive hands, accumulated scores, the target and tie-breaks. Hand Validate ownership and turns; apply plays, passes, announcements and hand completion. Board and scoring rules Check legal connections and open ends; calculate the credits associated with an action. Bot strategy Choose from legal moves using its own tiles and the public board. From a click to the next turn The player selects a tile and a destination in the React table. The interface checks that it is the human’s turn and that no required announcement or feedback is blocking input. The event handler calls hand.play(player, piece, branch). The engine checks the move and updates the hand, board and scoring state. An invalid move produces an error rather than a partially applied play. React renders the updated state: the tile’s new position, the open-end total, team scores and any result or announcement. A revision counter triggers a render after changes to the engine object. On a bot turn, a timer passes the public board, that bot’s own tiles and its legal moves to chooseBotTurn. Its chosen move goes through the same engine validation. Required decisions and feedback pause automatic play. This gives the local table immediate responses without a gameplay API, a database or a network round trip for each turn. The trade-off is that the match lives in browser memory: reloading the page does not restore a saved match.
Multiplayer architecture: the server owns the match Hiding opponents’ tiles in the interface is enough for the local experience, but the browser still holds that entire local match. Online play uses a different boundary: an Express server runs the same TypeScript engine and sends each player a filtered view. During a hand, that view contains the player’s own tiles, the public board and opponents’ tile counts. Other hands are revealed only when the hand ends.
Synchronization currently uses HTTP requests, with the browser polling the room every 800 milliseconds. A move carries the room revision and a request identifier. The server checks the account, seat, turn and move before applying it; repeated requests cannot score the same action twice. There is no WebSocket transport in this version.
Online play shares the rules engine with local play, but moves, persistence and access checks belong to the server.
Part of the online game Where it runs Tile selection, board rendering and feedback Each player’s React client Room seats, match state, rules and scoring The Express server Bot turns and required bot decisions Server timers using the shared bot strategies Human identity verification Google sign-in, validated by the server Profiles, sessions, room snapshots and completed results PostgreSQL on a persistent volume TV table A read-only React view from a revocable spectator link The bots keep their single-player profiles and strategies. Their decisions receive only their own tiles and public information, even though the authoritative engine runs on the server. Their turns do not depend on the room creator keeping a browser timer running.
A stale move is not a lost connection One intermittent “reconnecting” message turned out to have a more specific cause. If another action had already advanced the room, the server rejected the client’s old revision with HTTP 409. The interface treated that response as a disconnection, even though the server had answered normally.
The client now fetches the current room state after a revision conflict, without replaying the stale action. Actual network failures still show a connection warning, which clears after synchronization recovers. Tests cover both a failed action request and a failed refresh following a conflict.
A check of the Oracle host found available CPU, memory and disk capacity, no Galim container restarts or out-of-memory termination, and 30 successful API responses out of 30. That was a healthy sample at the time of inspection; it does not establish the cause of every past connection interruption.
Recover the table, then record the result Human profiles now survive application deployments. On a successful Google login, the server saves or updates the Google identity, name, email, optional profile image and login timestamps/count in PostgreSQL before issuing the session. An atomic update keeps concurrent logins from creating duplicate users.
Persistence now goes beyond profiles. Sessions and room snapshots survive application restarts. Snapshots preserve the current hand, score, decisions, substitutions and accepted request identifiers. The server restores that state instead of dealing another hand or applying a retried move again.
The runtime serializes room operations and commits changes to PostgreSQL before acknowledging them. A database ownership marker prevents a replaced process from continuing to write during deployment. If a commit fails with an uncertain outcome, the runtime stops serving room operations until recovery from the database. This remains a single active writer architecture, rather than a horizontally distributed game server.
Connection loss and voluntary departure have different rules. A disconnected player has 60 seconds before a bot temporarily takes over; returning restores control of the current hand. Confirming a voluntary departure makes the replacement permanent. If every human is absent, the match pauses instead of letting bots finish it alone. After five minutes without a return, the room closes without a winner. Watching on a TV does not extend that deadline, and a restart does not reset it.
Completed online matches feed private history and multiplayer rankings. History stores summaries, participants, rules and scores, not a tile-by-tile replay. Rankings separate all-human tables from tables involving bots or substitutions. The server records the result; it does not accept an online victory claimed by a browser.
Single-player matches started while signed in can also save a summary to that account. Because those results are calculated in the browser, they stay out of multiplayer rankings. Anonymous play remains available, and saving a completed result does not provide recovery of an unfinished local match.
A shared TV and a lobby for finding tables The host can now enable a spectator link that opens without Google sign-in. It shows the public board, score, moves, galo announcements and passes, without player controls. The server creates a separate projection and replaces account identifiers with seat identifiers; hiding elements in CSS would not protect the underlying data.
During play, spectators receive no private tiles. At the end of a hand, the remaining tiles are revealed so everyone can inspect the result, following the rule we confirmed after the initial spectator proposal. The next hand hides them again. The host can revoke the link, and enabling it again generates a new token.
The authenticated lobby adds public and private tables, with private as the default. People can search public tables by their players, request a seat and wait for the host to accept or decline. Concurrent requests cannot claim the same seat. This is table discovery; searching for available people outside those tables is still planned.
Events and the first payment experiment Event campaigns connect an online match to a physical giveaway. Each campaign has its own QR link, time window and stock. A signed-in participant must complete an eligible server-controlled match, winning or losing, to obtain a voucher. An authorized operator records the delivery, with one gift per account per campaign while stock lasts.
The interesting engineering problem is the last item: two operators must not deliver it twice, and retrying a delivery must not consume another unit. PostgreSQL transactions, unique records and stock audit entries protect that operation. The feature was deployed on October 26; actual event participation and physical distribution are separate from its automated validation.
A supporter package is also implemented with Stripe card checkout and AbacatePay Pix, verified webhooks and a badge/theme tied to the account. Payment and refund flows have been exercised in sandbox. Real sales remain disabled as of this update. That distinction matters: working integration code and test transactions are not a commercial launch.
Test complete hands Testing a domino game means checking whole sequences, not only individual moves. Recorded simulations let the tests replay turns and compare the final score and credits. Browser tests exercise complete hands through the table, including blocked games, announcements, and tie-breaks.
The October 26 event delivery passed 350 server tests across 45 suites and 98 browser end-to-end tests. Coverage includes online play, persistence, spectator views and concurrent voucher redemption. Earlier increments also exercised recovery across server restarts, private history, ranking separation and solo-result retries with real PostgreSQL. These are recorded checks from those deliveries, not a new execution of the application suites for this article update. Automated authentication uses a controlled provider; it complements the group’s real play experience.
What remains ahead The backlog includes finding available people, expanding the regional bot cast and supporting an explicit offline single-player experience. Commercial payments still need production activation. The implemented game already covers the table, its spectators and its results; the next decisions concern how people find it and keep returning.
summary: I had made games before, back when I was in college, but the idea for this one came during the pandemic. Dominoes are popular across Northern Brazil, including a point-scoring variant played in many homes. Galim is simply the name we gave this kind of game, not the name of the broader game category. Ralph and I play it with a set of regional rules, and turning those rules into software meant making each detail explicit: when a player may pass, how a hand ends, and how the score is credited.
title: Building Galim: A Domino Game from Northern Brazil

content:
The idea for Tribe Academy came from a recurring need I saw across companies: keeping internal courses organized and following up on learning as part of professional development plans (PDIs) and onboarding. Teams need a place to organize learning materials, guide people through clear next steps, and follow up on progress without losing sight of who can access what.
The authenticated workspace brings learning progress and the next action into the same view. This account has no enrolled paths yet.
Explore the published application at tribe.academy.tribesolutions.com.br/app. Access requires an invitation from an organization.
That meant building more than a catalog of courses. The platform brings together organizations, teams, memberships, learning paths, assignments, and progress. Authors can organize a path into modules and activities, while learners can see their missions and pick up where they left off. Managers can review submitted work and follow progress for the people and paths they are responsible for.
Designing for more than one organization The multi-company model shaped many of the product decisions. Each organization has its own people, teams, paths, and settings. Platform administration is a separate role: it can manage plans and domains without granting access to a customer’s learning content.
The free plan and organization limits also needed predictable behavior. When an organization reaches a limit, the platform should explain what happened and preserve its existing data. A plan change should not quietly delete learning materials or memberships.
Learning needs a next step A list of available paths is useful, but it does not always help someone decide what to do next. The personal mission view brings overdue work, returned activities, and upcoming deadlines forward. Inside a path, learners can resume an available activity, while completed work remains available for reference.
Authors can also choose between a list of activities and a map of learning steps. This changes how a path is presented while keeping its content and learner progress intact.
Architecture: from the browser to the data The application uses Next.js and TypeScript, with a shared Supabase backend for authentication, PostgreSQL and private file storage. The web application runs in a container managed through Coolify. A company’s hostname identifies its workspace; active membership and database authorization determine what a person can access inside it.
The main request and data boundaries. PDF delivery and authentication email use the separate flows described below.
Next.js Server Components load the page’s data on the server. Interactive components and forms send changes through Server Actions; route handlers handle operations such as opening a private PDF. The server-side Supabase client reads the user’s session cookies, so ordinary learning queries and database function calls run in that user’s context.
Boundary What crosses it Where it is checked Browser → Next.js Page requests, form fields and session cookies over HTTPS Session, input and workspace checks on the server. Next.js → Supabase data API Queries and RPC calls with the user’s session PostgreSQL row-level security and permission checks in database functions. Next.js → private Storage A request to sign a specific material’s object path User-visible material lookup and hostname scope before a privileged signing operation. Supabase Auth → email hook → Resend A signed authentication event, followed by an email delivery request Webhook signature, global budget reservation and idempotency. What happens when a learner completes a step The browser submits the enrollment, step, requested completion state and the revision it last read to a Server Action. The action resolves the signed-in user and active organization, then loads an enrollment belonging to that learner and organization. An identifier supplied by the browser is not sufficient authorization. It calls the PostgreSQL function set_step_completion through Supabase RPC, including p_expected_revision. Database rules validate the change; a stale revision becomes a conflict instead of silently overwriting newer work. The action revalidates the dashboard and study page, then redirects the browser to the step with success or error feedback. The next render reads persisted progress. This flow uses requests and server rendering; it does not rely on a live subscription. Text activities follow a similar path through submit_activity. If an activity changed in another session, the form retains the learner’s answer and asks them to refresh before retrying. That detail matters when someone has spent time writing a response.
Authentication and company isolation Login starts with a server-side request to Supabase Auth for an email link. The authentication callback establishes the session, and the Next.js proxy refreshes it for protected pages. The login request does not create an unknown user automatically; access is organized through invitations and membership.
The application resolves registered hostnames to organizations and restricts the workspace to the user’s active memberships. A cookie remembers the selected organization, but the server checks it against those memberships. PostgreSQL row-level security adds a second boundary for reads, while database functions enforce the permissions and rules for writes. Platform administration remains separate from access to a company’s learning content.
Opening a private PDF The browser first requests /api/materials/[id] from the application. The handler authenticates the user, looks up a material visible to that user, and checks that it belongs to the hostname’s organization when a tenant hostname is in use.
Only after those checks does a server-only Storage client create a signed URL valid for five minutes. The application redirects the browser to that URL, and Storage serves the PDF directly. The response uses private, no-store and no-referrer; the bucket stays private, and the privileged Storage credential stays on the server.
Email as a controlled backend operation Supabase Auth sends a signed event to /api/auth/send-email. The handler verifies the signature and reserves capacity in PostgreSQL before contacting Resend. Repeated events use an idempotency key, and delivery outcomes are recorded. Reserving capacity before the external request keeps concurrent deliveries subject to the same global limit, including failed attempts.
This separates authentication, authorization, file delivery and email into boundaries that can be tested independently, while keeping one application and a shared database manageable across companies.
Building the operational details Invitations, authentication, private PDF materials, organization domains, and email limits all affect whether the product can be operated safely. Those parts need clear boundaries: private files stay private, organization access follows active membership, and platform administration remains distinct from customer content.
The project uses Next.js and TypeScript, with Supabase for PostgreSQL, authentication, and storage. Unit, integration, and browser tests help validate the rules across the application. The recent work also added an audited global email limit for Academy authentication and invitations, so delivery failures and repeated events are handled deliberately.
Tribe Academy is an evolving product. The work so far has focused on making learning paths usable by teams and making the platform manageable across organizations, while keeping access and data ownership explicit.
summary: The idea for Tribe Academy came from a recurring need I saw across companies: keeping internal courses organized and following up on learning as part of professional development plans (PDIs) and onboarding. Teams need a place to organize learning materials, guide people through clear next steps, and follow up on progress without losing sight of who can access what.
title: Building Tribe Academy: A Learning Platform for Teams

content:
Anderson Pimentel: Senior SRE / Platform Engineer I’ve spent about ten years in engineering, most of them building and running platforms: Kubernetes in production, GitOps, AWS and observability.
